newsitem.title: INDIA: India's monsoon rains said to be on course.
newsitem.headline: India's monsoon rains said to be on course.

text.p: Indian weather officials and analysts on Monday dismissed a report that India's southwest monsoon rains have been receding, saying they were normal and there had been no effect on agriculture.
"It is a very, very happy scenario and we need not be worried" said S.R. Khalsi, a senior official of the Indian Meteorological Department.
"To the best of my understanding, it is not a panicky situation at all, there is no scare," said Ashok Gulati, an agriculture expert at the independent National Council of Applied Economic Research.
A report from Chicago on Friday quoted Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis as saying in his weather update that monsoonal activity in India had started to diminish considerably.

"This is a very unusual situation to occur during the middle of August," Davis wrote. "It means one of two things. Either the monsoonal activity is taking a break and it will rebuild later in August or the monsoon is starting to retreat."
But Khalsi disputed Davis's argument.
"I won't agree. We consider it as the nature of the monsoon. During the monsoon season there are weeks of good monsoon, there are weeks of bad monsoon," said Khalsi.
"But overall the nature of monsoon is good, there is nothing abnormal."
Khalsi said there was a rain deficiency in some areas that was likely to continue, particularly in the Vidarbha and Marathwada regions in western Maharashtra state.
But he said the situation in coastal areas in southern Andhra Pradesh state, which had earlier been deficient in rains, had improved.
"In the week ending August 13, there is a zero percent deficiency from the long term average for the country as a whole. Climatically whatever rains were expected had materialised," Khalsi said.
Gulati said the June-September monsoon was delayed by a week but the rainfall had been adequate.
"Wherever need was most, like in western India, there are no reports of sowing being affected," said Gulati.
He said the sowing of summer crops had already been done and reservoirs were fairly full.
Analysts said western forecasters had been banking on an adverse effect from the El Nino weather pattern in India.
They said although El Nino was said to be unfavourable to India, it had not had any adverse impact as in some Southeast Asian countries.

The government in a mid-season review of the monsoon said earlier this month that India was poised for the 10th successive normal monsoon with 29 of the 35 meteorological sub-divisions in the country receiving normal to excess rainfall.
"This year the adverse impact of El Nino, if any, is not yet visible and the monsoon circulation pattern is quite well established and healthy," the government statement said.
El Nino involves an increase in the water temperature off the western coast of South America which can disrupt weather patterns worldwide, creating drought in some areas and floods in others.
"There is statistical evidence that in the last 25 to 30 years there is no one-to-one correlation between El Nino and the Indian monsoon," said G.C. Iyer, a Bombay-based commodity analyst.
He said it was not unusual to see intermittent lulls in rainfall during the monsoon.
